pages.x: On 17 December 2010 Mohamed Bouazizi, a 26-year-old who sold fruit from a cart in the Tunisian town of Sidi Bouzid, set himself on fire after officials took away his scales and refused to hear his complaint. He died in January. Protests spread across Tunisia, filmed on phones and shared on Facebook.

After 23 years in power, Tunisia's president, Zine El Abidine Ben Ali, fled to Saudi Arabia on 14 January 2011. Across the Arab world people who had lived for decades under dictators watched, and wondered whether they could do the same. Everywhere the chant was the same: the people want the fall of the regime.

On 25 January Egyptians filled Tahrir Square in Cairo. They held it for eighteen days, fighting off the police and, one day, men charging on camels and horses. Christians stood guard while Muslims prayed. On 11 February Hosni Mubarak, president for thirty years, stepped down, and the square erupted in joy.

In Libya Muammar Gaddafi, in power for 42 years, sent his army against the rebels in Benghazi and promised to hunt them down house by house. The UN allowed air strikes to protect civilians, and NATO's planes helped the rebels win. In October Gaddafi was caught and killed, and Libya split between rival militias.

In Syria Bashar al-Assad met peaceful protests with bullets, and the country slid into a long civil war. In Yemen the president of 33 years was forced out, but Yemen too fell into war. In Bahrain, troops from Saudi Arabia helped to crush the protests.

In 2012 Egypt held its first free election for president, won by Mohamed Morsi of the Muslim Brotherhood. A year later, after huge protests against him, the army removed him, and its commander, Abdel Fattah el-Sisi, took power. Hundreds of Morsi's supporters were killed when their protest camps were cleared.

Tunisia, where it began, became a democracy, though after 2021 its president took more and more power. Elsewhere the hopes of 2011 ended in new strongmen, or in wars in Syria, Libya and Yemen. Still, the Arab Spring showed that ordinary people with phones could topple rulers who had seemed untouchable.
pts: Four rulers fell, in Tunisia, Egypt, Libya and Yemen
Ended in wars in Syria, Libya and Yemen
